Overshoot at\neach reversal is at most the last term used $\\to 0$, so the rearrangement converges to $s$.\n\n## What it kills\n\nSilent reindexing/reordering of infinite sums. \"Since addition is commutative...\" is\nvalid for finitely many terms only; for infinite sums it needs absolute convergence.\n\n## Debugging uses\n\n- Audit any proof that reorders a series, sums over an index set \"in a different order\",\n  swaps a double sum, or groups terms — each such step needs absolute convergence\n  (Fubini–Tonelli for sums) or an explicit argument.\n- Floating-point/parallel computing: reduction order changes results for near-cancelling\n  sums; this is the exact-arithmetic limit of that phenomenon.           "statement": "Two explicit finite witnesses, both found by exhaustive enumeration of all labeled preorders with |X| <= 5 (7331 of them), with all n! candidate linear orders checked per preorder.\n\nWITNESS 1 — the EXISTENCE of the linear order ≿_p fails.\nX = {a,b,c}, ≿ = {<a,a>,<a,b>,<b,a>,<b,b>,<c,c>}, i.e. a ~ b (mutual indifference, a ≠ b) and c incomparable to both. This is reflexive and transitive, hence a genuine preorder. Its incomparable ordered pairs are P = {<a,c>,<b,c>,<c,a>,<c,b>}, so P is NON-empty and the flagged sentence really is invoked here. Exhaustively checking all 3! = 6 linear orders on X (reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric, complete): the number extending ≿ is 0. Reason: any linear order ⊇ ≿ contains both <a,b> and <b,a>, and antisymmetry then forces a = b, contradiction. Claim says: for every p ∈ P a linear order ≿_p with ≿ ⊆ ≿_p and x ≿_p y exists; here the number of admissible ≿_p is 0 for 4 of the 4 pairs p ∈ P (0 out of 6 candidates each). Robustness: if \"linear order\" is read loosely as \"complete preorder / weak order\" (antisymmetry dropped), existence is rescued here (0 of 4 pairs fail), so this witness is specifically an antisymmetry failure.\n\nWITNESS 2 — the INTERSECTION IDENTITY fails, for EVERY admissible choice.\nX = {a,b}, ≿ = {<a,a>,<a,b>,<b,b>} (a strictly above b). ≿ is complete, so P = ∅ and the family {≿_p : p ∈ P} is empty; the intersection of an empty family of subsets of X² is X². Claim says intersection = ≿; here intersection = X² = {<a,a>,<a,b>,<b,a>,<b,b>} of size 4, while ≿ has size 3: |intersection| = 4 > |≿| = 3, the surplus pair being <b,a>, which is NOT in ≿ (indeed a ≻ b strictly). There is exactly one choice tuple (the empty one), so this was verified exhaustively, and it is independent of how \"linear order\" is read.\n\nFrequency in the swept space: existence (E) fails for 0/1/0/3/85/2290 preorders at n = 1..5, and the intersection identity fails for every admissible choice for 0/2/12/74/540 preorders at n = 1..5 (all of the latter being the complete-preorder, P = ∅, ≿ ≠ X² cases). Sanity: at n = 3 the 12 cases are exactly the 13 weak orders on 3 elements minus the all-indifferent relation X², as expected.
